ImageDescription.value:
Dans le Chettinad, on fabrique de manière artisanale des carreaux de ciment très brillants décorés de motifs variés (appelés "Athangudi Tiles" du nom du village du Chettinad qui a développé le procédé)

Ces carreaux ont été très utilisés dans les maisons de la communauté Chettiar.

Les dalles sont faites à partir d’argile que l’on trouve localement. Les couleurs sont mélangées à du ciment blanc et versées dans un moule sur une base de verre, ce qui permet de donne à la tuile une surface lisse et brillante. Après sa conception, la dalle est séchée au soleil puis plongée dans l’eau pendant quelques jours pour la durcir . Pour finir elle est remise à sécher au soleil.

extrait du site www.pixanne.net/wordpress/tag/chettinad/

ImageDescription.value:
Opening their company in 1850, George and Arthur Maw created lavish tiles out of their Edinburgh factory. This catalogue book was produced 17 years into the company’s history as a means to showcase their products. Each page is headed and labelled as ‘Maw and Co’s Encaustic Tiles/Tile Pavements, Benthall Works, Broseley, Shropshire’ with each title describing its true size once ordered and how many tiles are in a grouping shown to achieve a full/partial picture. Maw and Co still exists after many reincarnations of the company and can be found at www.mawandco…This company at one time was the largest producers of tiles in the world and served high status customers such as the Royal Family, Alexander II of Russia and many other dukes, earls and other institutions of high calibre.

Full record available at: images.is.ed.ac.uk/luna/servlet/s/zqc901

ImageDescription.value:
Part of a Medieval encaustic tile with an oxidised buff fabric. The fragment depicts a face on loggerhead or lion's head, in yellow against a mid red field. It bears similarites to Stopford design 25.7 (J Stopford, "Medieval Floor Tiles Of Northern England", 2005, p247, fig 24.1). There is one example of this at Fountains Abbey & four at Meaux Abbey, all done with the same stamp. They are both in northern England and, like Whalley Abbey, Cistercian foundations. Could date to any time between 1350 and 1600, but most likely to date between c1400 and c1550 AD.

The length is 63mm, width is 45mm, thickness is 23mm, and the weight is 73.77g.
